The electric guitar is a plucked instrument that needs external electrical amplification to sound at normal performing volume; it belongs to the chordophone lutes, Hornbostel–Sachs 513. It turns the vibration of the strings into an electrical signal with one or more pickups, and the speaker reproduces it; controls on the instrument and the amplifier adjust the timbre, and effects such as reverb, distortion and overdrive are used. The body may be hollow and semi-acoustic or solid, with a fixed bridge or a spring-loaded tremolo bridge, and the player can bend, tap, hammer, glide or use feedback. Jazz guitarists played single-note solos on it in large big bands; in rock it is divided into rhythm and lead guitar, and it also appears in pop, folk, country, blues and heavy metal.

A solid body has no resonant top, so it relies mainly on pickups, amplifier and speaker, and has less of the wolf tones and uncontrolled feedback that come with amplifying an acoustic guitar. The six strings are tuned E, A, D, G, B, E, and there are also seven-, eight- and twelve-string arrangements; bends, vibrato, tapping and glissando are used to change pitch and timbre.
